case_name: PETER JONES v ALLIED INVESTMENTS LIMITED
operative_excerpt: IN THE EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS AUTHORITY WELLINGTON I TE RATONGA AHUMANA TAIMAHI TE WHANGANUI Ā TARA ROHE [2025] NZERA 33 3213019 BETWEEN PETER JONES Applicant AND ALLIED INVESTMENTS LIMITED Respondent Member of Authority: Sarah Kennedy-Martin Representatives: Tim Cleary, counsel for the Applicant Susan Hornsby-Geluk, counsel for the Respondent Submissions received: 22 October and 18 November 2024 from Applicant 13 November 2024 from Respondent Determination: 23 January 2025 COSTS DETERMINATION OF THE AUTHORITY [1] In a determination dated 7 October 2024, I found that Mr Jones was successful in his constructive dismissal claim against Allied Investments Limited (AIL). Mr Jones was awarded lost wages, compensation, unpaid commission and wage arrears.1 [2] The Authority reserved the issue of costs and encouraged the parties to resolve any issue of costs between them. They have been unable to do so. [3] AIL filed a challenge in the Employment Court and in response to Mr Jones’ application for costs, submits the Authority’s consideration of costs should be deferred until after the challenge has been determined on the basis that costs ultimately follow the event. 1 Jones v Allied Investments Limited [2024] NZERA 595. [4] In the event the Authority decides costs should be determined, Mr Jones seeks an amount equivalent to the notional daily tariff for two days in the amount of $8,000.00 plus the Authority filing fee with an uplift of $1,200.00, on account of Mr Jones not being registered for GST. Costs [5] Costs are a matter of discretion. The discretion is to be exercised in accordance with principle and not arbitrarily. The main principle in the exercise of the discretion is that costs follow the event. If a party is successful, they will be entitled to an award of costs. Mr Jones was successful with his constructive dismissal personal grievance and is entitled to a consideration of costs. [6] The starting point for costs based on the Authority’s daily tariff is $4,500.00 for the first day and $3,500.00 for any following days. From that starting point the Authority can consider whether there are factors justifying an increase or decrease in costs. Analysis [7] The stay of execution ordered by the Court relates to the orders made by the Authority and it requires AIL to pay into Court the amounts ordered by the Authority to be paid to Mr Jones.2 It does not operate as a stay in relation to consideration of costs in the Authority. [8] It is usual for challenges to substantive determinations to be filed in the Employment Court before the Authority has decided costs. Once a costs determination is issued by the Authority, the party challenging the substantive determination can amend their statement of claim to include a challenge to the costs determination or either party can file a separate challenge to the costs determination.3 [9] The investigation meeting was held over two days. Mr Jones was the successful party and I consider an award in the amount equivalent to the daily tariff of $8,000.00 to be appropriate in this case. 2 [2024] NZEmpC 210, 2024 WL 4723356 3 See “ Employment Court Practice Directions” <www.employmentcourt.govt.nz> at No 11. [10] I decline to order an uplift for GST having regard to the purpose behind the notional daily tariff. I am satisfied that the costs incurred in this matter exceed the Authority’s notional daily tariff given how the matter progressed in the Authority. Summary of orders [11] Allied Investments Limited is ordered to pay Peter Jones costs in the sum of $8,000.00 and to reimburse the filing fee of $71.55 within 28 days of this determination. Sarah Kennedy-Martin Member of the Employment Relations Authority

case_name: JASMINE DE GROOT v THE ROYAL NEW ZEALAND SOCIETY FOR THE PREVENTION OF CRUELTY TO ANIMALS INCORPORATED
operative_excerpt: osed its mind to considering alternatives to dismissal. These were not the actions of a fair and reasonable employer. [57] For the reasons set out above, I conclude the RSPCA has not acted as a fair and reasonable employer could and Ms De Groot was unjustifiably dismissed. Was Ms De Groot unjustifiably disadvantaged by allegations being raised that were not pursued? The law [58] For her disadvantage claim to succeed, Ms De Groot must establish that one or more conditions of her employment was affected to her disadvantage by an unjustified action by the RSPCA.3 This means I need to determine whether Ms De Groot suffered a disadvantage in her employment, and – if so – whether this was caused by an action by the RSPCA and whether that action was unjustified. [59] The RSPCA’s actions are assessed in light of the test under s 103A of the Act and in particular, whether its actions and how it acted, were what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time the action occurred. [60] Ms De Groot says multiple allegations were raised by the RSPCA that were not pursued and this disadvantaged her. In submissions, Ms De Groot has raised new disadvantages around the failure to consider or account for her ADHD diagnosis, the timing of raising a further allegation while she was on stress leave, and escalating the recording issues to being one of two core allegations in a disciplinary context. Ms De Groot says the allegations caused her significant stress and worry and the micromanagement in relation to allegations that were later dropped was unnecessary. Ms De Groot says the RSPCA unjustifiably hung onto a “shopping basket” of low level concerns or minor matters which was unreasonable and not in good faith. [61] The RSPCA says the only disadvantage that has been clearly raised and advanced throughout the Authority’s proceedings relates to raising allegations which were not pursued following the preliminary meeting. The RSPCA says Ms De Groot should not be permitted to raise new disadvantage claims 4, but if she is, sufficient evidence has not been provided to substantiate her claims. The RSPCA says it was entitled to raise issues with Ms De Groot, and seek her response, and that it acted fairly and reasonably when it accepted her explanations and decided not to pursue certain allegations further. 3 ANZ National Bank Ltd v Doidge [2005] ERNZ 518 (EmpC). 4 In reliance on the general principle as to jurisdiction affirmed in McCulloch and Partners v Smith CA133/03, 3 December 2003. [62] Ms De Groot is not able raise new disadvantage claims through submissions. The claimed disadvantage relates to the RSPCA raising allegations that were not substantiated and not pursued. This action was not disadvantageous to Ms De Groot, or unjustified. There was no evidence to support that the allegations raised were completely without merit. It was appropriate for the RSPCA to raise its concerns with Ms De Groot, and to promptly discontinue any further action once an allegation was considered to be unsubstantiated. There was no unjustified action by the RSPCA in not pursuing these allegations, and to the contrary it would have been unfair and unjust of the RSPCA to have continued to investigate unsubstantiated concerns or allegations. I conclude Ms De Groot has not been unjustifiably disadvantaged by the RSPCA raising multiple allegations with her which were unsubstantiated and not pursued. Remedies [63] I have found Ms De Groot was unjustifiably dismissed from her employment and she is therefore entitled to an assessment of remedies. [64] Ms De Groot seeks: (a) Compensation under s 123(1)(c) of the Act for humiliation, loss of confidence, loss of dignity and injury to her feelings. (b) Reimbursement of lost wages under s 123 (1)(b) for lost wages. (c) Reimbursement of other money lost as a result of the grievance under s 123(1)(b). [65] She asks the Authority to consider an award of compensation at the higher end of the bands set by the Employment Court under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act5 but does not quantify an amount. [66] The RSPCA submits no order for compensation is warranted as it says Ms De Groot has provided limited evidence in support of harm (in particular, she has not provided any medical information), did not seek medical help or counselling, and she found new employment within a short period of time. It submits cases it says are analogous where awards of compensation were between a nominal amount of $1,000.00 5 As set out in Waikato District Health Board v Archibald [2017] NZEmpC 132, and Richora Group Limited v Cheng [2018] NZEmpC 132 and adjusted in GF Comptroller of the New Zealand Customs Services [2023] NZEmpC 101. and a maximum of $7,000.00. The RSPCA says an award to Ms De Groot should be at the lower end of Band 1 of the Employment Court’s bands, around $5,000.00. [67] The Employment Court recently confirmed that s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act does not contain an express or implied requirement for medical evidence to be produced to award anything other than modest loss.6 There is detailed evidence of the impact on Ms De Groot and medical evidence is not required to support her statements. I am not persuaded that a nominal amount of compensation is appropriate in this case for the reasons that follow. [68] The impact of losing her job has been devastating for Ms De Groot. She is a vet nurse, and her qualifications and experience were in animal care. She says after being dismissed, her life was turned upside down. Her mother described her state of mind as “broken” and “depressed” – the loss of her dream job was devastating, and Ms De Groot lost confidence and doubted herself. She had a huge fear of rejection by her friends and former workmates, and from potential employers. Although Ms De Groot found a new job through an MSD advertisement, the job is not in her field or career path and only pays minimum wage. She is in debt to her parents, and continues to rely on them for financial assistance. Ms De Groot says she continues to feel grief, uncertainty and betrayal over what she experienced in her employment. [69] The impact of losing a job in a sector with a deeply held ethos of caring for animals would, I accept, be devastating. One HR manager referred to working for the RSPCA as heart-centric work with heart-centric people. Ms De Groot has given significant and compelling evidence detailing the impact the summary dismissal has had on her from an emotional and financial perspective, and of suffering substantial humiliation, loss of confidence, loss of dignity and injury to her feelings. [70] I have considered the general range of compensation awards in other cases. Based on the evidence of emotional impact on Ms De Groot as expressed in her statement and the statement of her mother, and standing back to objectively assess the impact as best I can, I consider an appropriate award of compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act is $20,000.00 (subject to any reduction for contribution). 6 Keighran v Kensington Tavern Limited [2024] NZEmpC 28; see also Maddigan v Director General of Conservation [2019] NZEmpC 190 Lost wages [71] Under s 123(1)(b) of the Act, the Authority is able to order that the employee be reimbursed a sum equal to the whole or part of any wages or other money lost by the employee as a result of the grievance. Section 128 of the Act provides that the Authority must order the employer to pay lost remuneration or 3 months’ ordinary time remuneration where the Authority determines an employee has a personal grievance and has lost remuneration as a result of the grievance, although there is a discretionary power in s 128(3) of the Act to award a greater sum. [72] When assessing the appropriate award for lost remuneration, the applicable principles are that full financial losses set the upper limit on an award of compensation, and there is no automatic entitlement to full compensation. Moderation is required. Precision is difficult and awards of compensation “will inevitably involve a broad brush approach”.7 [73] Ms De Groot claims: (i) Lost wages for the period she was out of work from 20 November 2023 to 14 January 2024 of $8,415.20 (gross). (ii) Lost wages from between 14 January 2024 to early October 2024 being the shortfall between what she would have earned at the RSPCA and what she earned in her new minimum wage job of $7,192.20 (gross). (iii) Lost money being the debt owed to her parents for mortgage and bill payments of $4,898.29 (net), continuing at a rate of $218.00 per month. [74] The RSPCA submits its decision to terminate Ms De Groot’s employment was substantively justified and therefore no award for lost wages ought to be made. It also submits Ms De Groot is not entitled to full reimbursement of her lost remuneration, because it is disproportionate to the circumstances. The RSPCA says Ms De Groot has not provided evidence of the benefit she obtained after she was dismissed or roles she applied for, and has not sufficiently attempted to mitigate her losses. In summary, the RSPCA says there is insufficient evidence to enable the Authority to assess to what extent Ms De Groot has suffered a loss of wages and whether she could have avoided that loss. 7 Sam’s Fukuyama Food Services Ltd v Zhang [2011] NZCA 608, para 36. [75] Ms De Groot claims total loss of wages for the first two months after her employment ended, amounting to $8,415.20 (gross) before she secured new employment. I accept that for a third month she continued to suffer a loss as a result of the grievance being the shortfall between her old wage and her new wage, of approximately $777.54 (gross).8 Her total loss over the three month period following the end of her employment was therefore $9,192.74 (gross). I consider that is a fair and proportionate award, and I order the RSPCA to make that payment to Ms De Groot. [76] I consider it appropriate to make an award for lost wages under s 123(1)(b) of the Act, notwithstanding Ms De Groot may have received benefit payments as confirmed by her mother.9 The principle discussed in Judea Tavern10 is that liability to pay wages or compensation for wages rests with the employer and other compensation in the nature of benefits, does not displace this liability. Consequently, the appropriate approach is to put any question of repayment of benefits to one side in terms of my assessment of an appropriate award under s 123(1)(b) and I decline to make any deduction from my calculation of lost remuneration for benefits in this case. [77] The RSPCA says the Authority is not able to order other amounts claimed by Ms De Groot because these were not raised in her statement of problem. I accept the RSPCA’s submission, and decline to make any additional orders. Contribution [78] In deciding the nature and extent of remedies for any personal grievance, I must consider the extent to which Ms De Groot may have acted in a way that contributed to the situation that gave rise to her grievance.11 [79] The RSPCA says Ms De Groot’s conduct was causative, blameworthy and contributory and an appropriate reduction would be 50 percent. [80] Ms De Groot says she has always accepted she failed to record some standard flea and worming treatments, and this was resolved prior to the disciplinary events of September and October. She says no actions or inactions of hers have led to her personal grievances and no contribution should be found. 8 $194.38 per week for 4 weeks. 9 Brief of Evidence, Fiona De Groot, paragraph 26. 10 Judea Tavern Limited v Patricia Jesson [2017] NZEmpC 82, at [40]. 11 Employment Relations Act 2000, section 124. [81] The Employment Court has recently succinctly summarised the key principles relating to contribution as follows:12 (i) First, the Court must be satisfied that the actions of the employee contributed to the situation that gave rise to the personal grievance; if so (ii) Second, an assessment of whether the employee’s actions “require” a reduction in the remedies that would otherwise have been awarded. [82] The Court also stated:13 The primary considerations when determining whether a particular action should result in a reduction for contribution are causation and proportionality. [83] The Court has endorsed an approach where a reduction of 50 percent sits at the higher end with 25 percent representing a still significant reduction. [84] Based on the evidence before the Authority, I find Ms De Groot did not contribute to the situation giving rise to her grievance and therefore no reduction in remedies is appropriate. Subsequently discovered misconduct [85] The RSPCA says Ms De Groot’s discussions with her colleagues and volunteers about the disciplinary process including comments about Ms Moore wanting her out of the workplace amounted to a breach of good faith and fidelity and the Authority should exercise its discretion not to award remedies. I do not consider this to amount to subsequent misconduct, and I decline to exercise my discretion to not award remedies. Charitable status of the organisation [86] The RSPCA submits that its status as a charitable organisation which is entirely reliant on donations and funding to continue promoting the welfare of animals and providing care to vulnerable animals, means any order for remedies would be likely to damage the organisation unfairly or unnecessarily and impact its charitable purpose. [87] There is insufficient evidence before the Authority of any impact or likely impact on the RSPCA. I consider that because this submission is unsupported by any 12 Keighran v Kensington Tavern Limited [2024] NZEmpC 28; see also Maddigan v Director General of Conservation [2019] NZEmpC 190 at [71] – [76]. 13 Keighran v Kensington Tavern Limited [2024] NZEmpC 28 at [17]. evidence, there is no basis for the Authority to reduce an otherwise appropriate award of remedies. Orders [88] I have found Ms De Groot was unjustifiably dismissed by the RSPCA. [89] I order that within 28 days of the date of this determination The Royal New Zealand Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Incorporated is to pay Jasmine De Groot: (i) Compensation for humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act in the amount of $20,000.00. (ii) Reimbursement of lost wages under s 123(1)(b) and s 128(1)(b) of the Act in the amount of $9,192.74 (gross). Costs [90] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [91] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, Ms De Groot may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum the RSPCA will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [92] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.14 Natasha Szeto Member of the Employment Relations Authority 14 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

(4) If the employer or representative is satisfied that the request was made or that the behaviour took place, the employer or representative must take whatever steps are practicable to prevent any repetition of such a request or of such behaviour. [50] Submissions on behalf of FTT also referred to s 118 of the Act, which in this matter would apply if I were to find SPM had not taken, after a complaint under s 117(2) of the Act, whatever steps are practicable to prevent the repetition of behaviour described under s 108(1)(b) of the Act. Submissions of the parties [51] Submissions for FTT said they were sexually harassed in their employment with SPM in relation to the incident involving a co-worker, HWZ, discussed in relation to the claim of unjustified disadvantage above. The requirement for SPM to inquire into the facts under s 117(3) of the Act was said to have been met as: a. HWZ was FTT’s co-worker and FTT alleged HWZ’s actions involved language and physical behaviour of a sexual nature in terms of the requirements of s 108(1)(b) – combined this met the requirements of s 117(1)(b); and b. FTT had complained to DLW as required under s 117(2). [52] In terms of s 117(4) of the Act SPM’s conclusion it was not satisfied behaviour which constituted sexual harassment was said to be defective as SPM had failed to gather all relevant facts and had failed to apply the limited facts to the statutory definition of sexual harassment in s 108(1)(b) of the Act. SPM were said to have inappropriately applied an: objective test in company policy – “Sexual Harassment is any unwelcome sexual attention that a “reasonable person” would consider to be offensive, humiliating or intimidating”. [53] As a consequence, FTT said SPM “prevented itself from satisfying itself that the behaviour took place and taking whatever steps practicable to prevent repetition of the behaviour required by subsection 117(4)” and under s 118(1)(b) of the Act “failed to take the necessary prevention steps potentially leaving itself and other employees open to a repeat behaviour in the future”. Submissions for FTT then said as they “never returned to work for fear of repetition” s118 could not apply and their “recourse therefore reverts to the disadvantage grievance and the unjustifiable dismissal grievance”. [54] Submissions for SPM said s 117 of the Act did not apply as SPM had found no sexual harassment however if it had then there had been no repeated behaviour by HWZ of the kind described under s 108(1)(b) of the Act and SPM “had taken practical steps to prevent a repetition of the behaviour albeit in a non disciplinary” way. SPM also said as FTT did not return to work, SPM’s actions could not be put to test. SPM acknowledged “[FTT] was entitled to view the behaviour of [HWZ] subjectively”, including taking into account contextual information which SPM did not know of. SPM said however its actions need to be viewed objectively as with any personal grievance claim, applying s 103A of the Act. Analysis [55] I find FTT was subjected to behaviour covered by s 117(1)(b) of the Act and made a complaint under s 117(2) of the Act. DLW then undertook an investigation on behalf of SPM, as required under s 117(3) of the Act. [56] As discussed in paragraphs [29] to [38] above, I have found FTT was unjustifiably disadvantaged by SPM’s failure to sufficiently investigate FTT’s complaint they had been sexually harassed. The requirements of s 117(4) of the Act differ and relate to situations where an employer finds unwelcome behaviour occurred. These requirements are linked to s 118 of the Act in relation to repeated behaviour. [57] In this case, I consider SPM’s investigation was deficient and SPM misdirected itself in relation to what behaviour could be sexual harassment and in downplaying the subjective significance of HWZ’s actions and their impact on FTT. SPM did however inquire into the matter as required by s 117(3) of the Act and while potentially erroneously concluding the behaviour did not meet the definition of sexual harassment, SPM did take steps to prevent the repetition of HWZ’s unwelcome behaviour as required by s 117(4) of the Act. [58] Submissions for FTT acknowledged s 118 of the Act could not apply due to FTT not returning to work, meaning recourse lies elsewhere. I agree and consider FTT’s complaints have been adequately addressed by consideration of their unjustified disadvantage and unjustified dismissal grievances. Conclusion: FTT has not established breaches by SPM of ss 117 or 118 of the Act [59] I find FTT has not established SPM breached its obligations under ss 117 or 118 of the Act. What remedies should be awarded to FTT in relation to unjustified disadvantage? [60] Having determined FTT was unjustifiably disadvantaged, I need to consider what remedies should follow. FTT sought lost wages under s 123(1)(b) of the Act for two periods, first for the unjustified disadvantage claim from when they left work on 6 May 2022 until when SPM became aware of their resignation on 16 August 2022, and then for the unjustified constructive dismissal claim for a further three months. FTT also sought compensation of between $10,000 and $40,000 for hurt and humiliation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act. Finally FTT sought recommendations be made to SPM under s 123(1)(ca) and (d) of the Act. [61] As I have found only FTT’s unjustified disadvantage claim to have been established, remedies for lost wages are limited to those connected to this claim. FTT said this claim inclusive of lost holiday pay and employer’s Kiwisaver contributions if applicable were “estimated circa $12,000”. FTT said compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act should take into account: the sensitivity (sexual nature) of the matter, the respondent’s lack of regard for the complainant throughout, the respondent’s defective investigatory response to its own policy and its section 117 duty under the Act, its low level of investigatory acumen by substandard investigatory knowledge and skills, a substandard understanding of sexual harassment under the Act, no evidence of staff training or provision of staff awareness, failure to in good faith communicate adequately with the applicant throughout. [62] SPM said FTT was not entitled to remedies for lost wages as they “did not lose wages as a result of … walking out on 6 May” as FTT: left and took sick leave until it was exhausted and never returned to work. [Their] departure had nothing to do with the employers conduct and doesn’t entitle [them] to claim remedies for unjustified action. [63] SPM also said FTT was not entitled to remedies under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act “just because [they] didn’t agree with the outcome of the employers investigation”. [64] I find FTT is entitled to lost wages for the period from when they left work on 6 May 2022 until when they actually resigned, which email evidence shows occurred on 29 June 2022. While there was some confusion over whether this email from FTT to a representative of SPM was received, it appears clear to me FTT was unsatisfied with discussions between their then representative and SPM’s advocate, and acted to end their employment on this date, which I consider breaks the causation of loss. FTT’s employment agreement required notice but provided payment may be forfeited if notice was not worked out, which occurred here and I consider disqualifies them for additional losses for the notice period. [65] There appears also to be a period when FTT was on sick leave until at least 14 May 2022, based on a letter dated 13 May 2022 from DLW communicating the outcome of their investigation and expressing the expectation SPM would be returning to work on 23 May 2022. To the extent SPM provided FTT with paid sick leave, there would have been no loss, so any paid sick leave should be taken into account when calculating the lost wages due. [66] As I do not have sufficient evidence to calculate lost wages, I order SPM to calculate and pay to FTT an amount for lost wages under s 123(1)(b) of the Act equivalent to their pay due from 6 May 2022 until 29 June 2022, less any amounts of paid sick leave provided during this period, including any additional holiday pay and employer Kiwisaver contributions applicable. If the parties cannot agree on this amount, they may revert to the Authority for further orders. [67] FTT is also entitled to compensation under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act in relation to the deficiencies in SPM’s investigation process which led to the finding FTT was unjustifiably disadvantaged. FTT said they had “really bad anger issues” over what had occurred including the incident with HWZ but also were impacted by how SPM’s investigation was conducted and ultimately concluded they could not safely return to work. They said this “made me feel like shit” and referred to contextual information which related to the impacts on them. FTT said they would still be working at SPM if the matter was handled better. [68] I acknowledge FTT’s evidence was of significant impacts on them however this evidence was mixed as to the causes of those impacts, referring to the actions of HWZ, the inadequate investigation by SPM, the ending of FTT’s employment in a job they said they were really good at and appeared to have enjoyed. FTT’s evidence also referred to the impact of contextual information which SPM was not aware of until the investigation meeting, which while traumatic, SPM could not be responsible for. [69] Based on FTT’s evidence of the impacts of SPM’s unjustified actions on them, related to FTT’s unjustified disadvantage claim, taking into account comparable cases, I consider an award of compensation of $15,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act is appropriate, before considering contribution. [70] FTT sought recommendations under s 123(1)(ca) and (d) of the Act that SPM: a. revise its Discrimination and Sexual Harassment policy to update the definition of sexual harassment to be consistent with the Act and to set out investigation steps; b. update employment agreements; and c. train employees on investigating sexual harassment and provide “general training for all staff to raise awareness that behaviour of a sexual nature is wholly inappropriate in the workplace”. [71] SPM did not directly address whether recommendations were appropriate, although its submissions implied no recommendations were appropriate. In DLW’s letter dated 13 May 2022 communicating the outcome of their investigation they said “Whilst we have not found any evidence of sexual harassment occurring, we have taken this opportunity to review our company policies and procedures and have found that they are up to date and do not require any updates”. [72] I recommend under s 123(1)(ca) of the Act that SPM review its Discrimination and Sexual Harassment policy to update the definition of sexual harassment to be consistent with s 108 of the Act and in particular to reflect sexual harassment includes under s 108(1)(b) of the Act actions which “directly or indirectly subjects the employee to behaviour that is unwelcome or offensive to that employee”, which is a subjective test. I consider SPM’s Discrimination and Sexual Harassment policy, quoted in submissions at paragraph [52] above, is more consistent with an objective test of whether behaviour constitutes sexual harassment. [73] I decline to make the other recommendations sought by FTT, as I am not satisfied they are required. SPM may wish to consider however in communicating with its staff about any changes to its Discrimination and Sexual Harassment policy that these are being made to reinforce awareness that behaviour of a sexual nature is wholly inappropriate in SPM’s workplace. Should remedies be reduced (under s 124 of the Act) for blameworthy conduct by FTT that contributed to the situation giving rise to their grievance? [74] I am required to consider if remedies should be reduced (under s 124 of the Act) for blameworthy conduct by FTT that contributed to the situation giving rise to their grievance. [75] While FTT and IOT could have followed up on the meeting with DWL and SPM’s advocate on 12 May 2022 differently, which may have created an opportunity to mitigate in part FTT’s lost wages, I do not consider this meets the requirements of blameworthy conduct by FTT that contributed to the situation giving rise to their grievance. The basis for FTT’s unjustified disadvantage grievance was SPM’s failure to sufficiently investigate FTT’s complaint they had been sexually harassed and I do not consider FTT contributed in a blameworthy manner to the shortcomings in SPM’s investigation process. [76] No reduction is made for contribution accordingly. Summary of outcome [77] I have found: a. FTT was unjustifiably disadvantaged by Sinclair Pryor Motors Limited’s (SPM) failure to sufficiently investigate FTT’s complaint they had been sexually harassed; b. FTT has not established their resignation was an unjustified constructive dismissal, as I do not consider it was reasonably foreseeable FTT would resign in the circumstances; and c. FTT has not established SPM breached its obligations under ss 117 or 118 of the Employment Relations Act 2000 (the Act) in relation to sexual harassment by a person other than their employer. Orders [78] For the above reasons I order SPM to within 28 days of the date of this determination: a. calculate and pay FTT an amount for lost wages under s 123(1)(b) of the Act equivalent to their pay due from 6 May 2022 until 29 June 2022, less any amounts of paid sick leave provided during this period, including any additional holiday pay and employer Kiwisaver contributions applicable. If the parties cannot agree on this amount, they may revert to the Authority for further orders; and b. compensation of $15,000 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act without deduction. [79] I also recommend under s 123(1)(ca) of the Act SPM review its Discrimination and Sexual Harassment policy to update the definition of sexual harassment to be consistent with s 108 of the Act. Costs [80] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [81] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, FTT may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum SPM will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [82] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors require an adjustment upwards or downwards.6 [83] As the investigation meeting for this matter took most of one day, concluding mid-afternoon, my preliminary view is the notional daily rate for one day is the appropriate starting point for a determination of costs. There is also no indication that Mr Lugo-Sharpe was authorised by Ms Aguirre to raise a personal grievance claim on her behalf when he was communicating with the Labour Inspector after the ending of his employment. [23] As such, I do not consider Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s correspondence with the Labour Inspectorate to be relevant or helpful in answering the question as to whether Ms Aguirre raised personal grievance claims with her employer KAH within the statutory timeframes. Claim 1.1 in the Statement of Problem – that Ms Aguirre was repeatedly overlooked for promotion to a higher position [24] My view is that the undated refusal of promotion grievance referred to by Mr Lugo-Sharpe is the same as the claim set out at paragraph 1.1 of the statement of problem. [25] Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s description is consistent with the detail given by Ms Aguirre in her statement of problem, and is also consistent with the details given by KAH in its own replies. [26] Having said this, there is no dispute that Ms Aguirre herself had raised this grievance directly with KAH on 28 January 2022. A letter from KAH dated 10 February 2022 acknowledges the raising of this grievance, and records that Mr Rashid met with her to discuss, but despite this she requested a formal response. The letter proceeds to set up a formal meeting accordingly on 14 February. [27] KAH says that this meeting was held with Ms Aguirre on 14 February 2022, and resolved matters by way of discussion, with Mr Rashid and Mr Kulkarni agreeing to promote her to the role of Banquets Operations Manager. Meeting notes provided by KAH indicate that Ms Aguirre accepted this promotion and stated that she considered the matter resolved. [28] There is no subsequent correspondence from Ms Aguirre on this subject. The next time this matter was drawn to KAH’s attention was some 18 months later, by Mr Halse’s email dated 12 June 2023 set out above, which refers specifically to this grievance by way of Ms Aguirre’s letter of 28 January 2022 and seeks her “full personnel file”. No explanation for the delay was provided, either then or now. [29] There is no dispute that this grievance was raised within time. I have considered whether this should be read as a dispute that this grievance was not resolved to Ms Aguirre’s satisfaction, but this is not the claim made in her statement of problem, or in the email from Mr Halse, which appears to rely on the original claim despite the intervening actions by KAH. I consider this significant. [30] I also consider it significant that there is no contemporaneous correspondence from Ms Aguirre following on from her grievance letter of 28 January, an intervening meeting with Mr Rashid where she required a formal response, the response letter of 10 February, and the meeting of 14 February. Ms Aguirre had expressed herself clearly and firmly, and KAH had responded positively, by providing her with a formal response, both a formal and an informal meeting, and the promotion she requested. If for some reason Ms Aguirre had not been satisfied by the response, it was clearly open to her to continue to advocate for what she wanted, but KAH’s position is that after discussion, it resolved matters by agreeing that she should have the promotion that she requested. [31] In these circumstances, I find it more likely than not that, although properly raised, this matter was resolved at the time. No grievance was raised about the resolution either then or now. In these circumstances, I find that Ms Aguirre cannot properly progress the claim set out in paragraph 1.1 of the statement of problem. She is estopped from raising this claim again after its resolution to her benefit and satisfaction, and she has never raised any claim about that resolution. Claim 1.2 in the Statement of Problem – that Ms Aguirre was subjected to bullying behaviours which were not investigated or addressed [32] The April 2022 claim referred to by Mr Lugo-Sharpe as well as the undated performance review claim referred to by him are generally similar to the claim set out at paragraph 1.2 of the statement of problem. [33] Unlike the undated refusal of promotion claim, there is no claim that Ms Aguirre raised these concerns in a formal way. KAH says that the first it was aware of these claims was on the filing of the statement of problem, which is dated 15 December 2023. This is more than a year after the ending of Ms Aguirre’s employment on 18 November 2022. Ms Aguirre relies on Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s witness statement to explain how and when she raised her grievances. [34] In relation to the April 2022 claim, Mr Lugo-Sharpe states that the grievance was that at an unspecified time, some unspecified action occurred that Ms Aguirre told him was “abuse”. He said he raised this with his manager and the conduct was denied. Ms Aguirre took no further action relating to this matter until the filing of her statement of problem on 15 December 2023, which raised a general bullying claim which is not on all fours with Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s witness statement. [35] Clearly the filing of the statement of problem on 15 December 2023 is well outside the period of 90 days from even the end of April 2022. It does not assist in ascertaining if the April 2022 claim was properly raised. [36] The court has held that: For an employer to be able to address a grievance as the legislation contemplates, the employer must know what to address….What is important is that the employer is made aware sufficiently of the grievance to be able to respond as the legislative system mandates2. [37] Mr Lugo-Sharpe does not give any details as to what occurred that Ms Aguirre considered to be “abuse”. KAH is not able to consider such a complaint, or take any steps to potentially address or resolve it, in the absence of detail as to what Ms Aguirre considered to have been wrong. Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s witness statement falls short of providing any level of detail which would enable a grievance to be raised with KAH. [38] I am equally concerned about the lack of dates provided by Mr Lugo-Sharpe. He does not state when Ms Aguirre “reported” this matter to him, he says only that she told him that the occurrence of this unspecified matter was sometime in the month of April 2022, and he does not say when he raised this with his manager. This lack of detail again means that KAH is not able to respond sufficiently. It is not enough for KAH to be put in the position of having to make its “best guess” about these matters. [39] Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s witness statement (even taken at face value) falls short of demonstrating that this grievance was properly raised. [40] I will now consider the undated performance review claim. Mr Lugo-Sharpe says that Ms Aguirre reported to him that Mr Kulkarni had engaged in “abusive and threatening behaviour” at a performance review meeting. Mr Lugo-Sharpe does not state what this behaviour was, or when the alleged meeting occurred, when Ms Aguirre raised these concerns with him, or when he raised them with his own manager. Both the lack of detail and the lack of any reference to dates suggest that this grievance has not been properly raised. 2 Creedy v Commissioner of Police [2006] ERNZ 517 at [36]. [41] I have also taken into account that the undated performance review claim is not mentioned by Ms Aguirre in her statement of problem, and is not supported by two contemporaneous emails that she has provided mentioning Mr Kulkarni. [42] The first email is dated 15 December 2021. In it, Ms Aguirre asks that she is not put on split shifts. She then says: Abhijeet (Kulkarni) kept walking behind me or coming to me telling me do this, don’t do this….I have been pulled out of my shift to do something else and I’m doing it correctly why I have someone in my ear telling me what I’m doing it’s not right. He didn’t even thank me… [43] This is referred to at paragraph 2.6 of the statement of problem as a concern with split shifts and “giving inconsistent instructions”. [44] The second email from Ms Aguirre mentioning Mr Kulkarni is dated 3 February 2022. She states: Abhijeet has been pushing us all with the workload and the wage cost…even calling us in the middle of a shift to tell us when need to go home….We also told Antony [Lugo- Sharpe] about the problems of communication that they have with Abhijeet….I’m very disappointed of how disorganised we are. I don’t want people to be overworked…Please don’t share this email with anyone. [45] This is referred to at paragraph 2.12 of the statement of problem as “unrealistic workloads and bullying behaviours by Abhijeet”, and “poor time management and poor communication from Abhijeet”. [46] Ms Aguirre then met with Mr Rashid and Mr Kulkarni on 14 February 2022, resulting in her being given a promotion. The meeting notes provided by KAH record that Mr Rashid then stated “all duty managers should equally do split shifts. I would like to see a flow through in the roster”. Mr Kulkarni acknowledged this, and it was at this point that Ms Aguirre accepts that the matter was resolved. [47] Taking all this into consideration, I find that Ms Aguirre did not raise a valid personal grievance about bullying behaviours that were not investigated or addressed. There is insufficient evidence that Ms Aguirre raised any issues about “bullying” or behaviour that might amount to that. There is evidence that Ms Aguirre raised some concerns about split shifts, workload, and communication, although she also asked that these concerns not be shared. There is also evidence that Ms Aguirre’s concrete concerns about shifts and the sharing of workload were discussed and addressed by Mr Rashid and Mr Kulkarni and that she accepted this. Mr Lugo-Sharpe’s witness statement contains no details that would suggest otherwise, or which amount to the raising of a timely and valid personal grievance claim about bullying that had gone unaddressed. [48] In these circumstances, I find that Ms Aguirre cannot properly progress the claim set out in paragraph 1.2 of the statement of problem. Claim 1.3 in the Statement of Problem – that Ms Aguirre was unjustifiably disadvantaged by a failure to provide rest and meal breaks [49] There is no indication that Ms Aguirre raised any claim with KAH about rest and meal breaks prior to her statement of problem. [50] This was not mentioned in the contemporaneous correspondence that I have already referred to, and is not mentioned by Mr Lugo-Sharpe in his witness statement. [51] Instead, there is evidence that Ms Aguirre complained about split shifts, and Mr Rashid spoke with her about ensuring this type of work was shared equally among the duty managers which Ms Aguirre agreed with. These matters were not referred to again until they were mentioned in the statement of problem, and even then, the statement of problem raises no claims in this regard. [52] This does not suggest either an ongoing grievance, or that any concerns were raised about rest and meal breaks within time. [53] In the absence of any evidence that Ms Aguirre raised this concern at all prior to the filing of the statement of problem more than 12 months after the ending of her employment, I find it more likely than not that these claims have not been validly raised. Claim 1.4 in the Statement of Problem – that Ms Aguirre was constructively dismissed [54] There is no indication that Ms Aguirre raised any claim with KAH about her dismissal prior to her statement of problem. [55] Mr Lugo-Sharpe does not mention it, which is to be expected as his employment came to an end some six months prior to the ending of Ms Aguirre’s own employment. [56] There is contemporaneous email correspondence from Ms Aguirre to KAH about the ending of her employment. It is not disputed that Ms Aguirre resigned by email on 18 November 2022. Contemporaneous correspondence indicates that this was not a sudden decision by Ms Aguirre. She had first tendered her resignation on 30 June 2022, and the text of that email describes her work in a positive way. KAH did not rush to accept Ms Aguirre’s resignation, but rather engaged in discussion with her about how she could be supported to stay in her employment, as shown by the subsequent agreement that Ms Aguirre take 2 months planned leave instead from September to October to visit her home country before returning to her employment. This suggests that KAH was active, responsive, and constructive, and that Ms Aguirre was a valued employee. [57] Ms Aguirre then took the agreed leave, and following this, decided not to return to work and re-confirmed her resignation. In that second email on 18 November 2022, she again refers in positive terms to the efforts made to support her and states “I’m really sorry I know you all have made an effort waiting for me but I’m not ready to work at the moment”. There is nothing to suggest that Ms Aguirre was dissatisfied with the way her employment was ending, or that she felt she could not return from her negotiated leave for reasons connected to KAH’s conduct. In fact, Ms Aguirre’s negotiation of a substantial amount of leave so she could travel home as an alternative to resigning suggests a willingness to maintain a good employment relationship. [58] Neither the 30 June 2022 email nor the 18 November 2022 email can reasonably be said to raise a personal grievance claim of constructive dismissal. The first time this claim was raised was in the statement of problem dated 15 December 2023. Ms Aguirre’s employment ended on 18 November 2022. This is clearly well beyond the 90-day period provided for the raising of personal grievances in s 114 of the Act. [59] For completeness, Ms Aguirre has not raised any claim that exceptional circumstances applied, however I have considered this also. There is no evidence of any barrier to Ms Aguirre raising her claims at an earlier stage. The evidence of communications from her indicate to the contrary, that she was willing and able to raise her concerns, hold her ground and insist on a formal response rather than an informal one, and actively negotiate alternative outcomes that were objectively beneficial to her. [60] As there is no evidence that Ms Aguirre raised her personal grievance claim of constructive dismissal within 90 days of the ending of her employment, I find that this claim cannot proceed in the Authority. Orders [61] The personal grievance claims set out at paragraph 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, and 1.4 of the statement of problem cannot be progressed for the reasons set out above. [62] As these are the only claims raised by Ms Aguirre, the matter is therefore dismissed. Costs [63] Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. [64] If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, the respondent may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum, the applicant will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. [65] The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.3 Claire English Member of the Employment Relations Authority 3 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

operative_excerpt: that a penalty may be imposed for a breach of s 130(1) of the Act. Section 75(2)(e) of the HA03 provides that a maximum penalty of $10,000.00 may be imposed on a person who has breached s 81 of the HA03, by failing to keep holiday a leave records. Relevant law When assessing penalties the Authority is required to take into account the factors set out in s 133A of the Act. The Authority has also been guided by the Employment Court decisions in Borsboom (Labour Inspector) v Preet PVT Limited and Warrington Discount Tobacco Limited7 as summarised by the Employment Court in Nicholson v Ford8 and A Labour Inspector v Daleson Investment Limited.9 Objects of the Act Section 4B of the Act reflected the importance of an employer keeping legally compliant and accurate employment records relating to minimum entitlement provisions as being one of the three “key provisions” accompanying the Act’s objects. Section 4B of the Act required employers to keep records in sufficient detail to demonstrate compliance with minimum entitlement provisions, as defined in s 5 of the Act. Section 4B(2) of the Act provided that obligation was in addition to the requirements of any other provisions, such as ss 65 and 130 of the Act and s 81 of the HA03, relating to record keeping. One of the objects in s 3 of the Act is to recognise the need for trust and confidence and good faith behaviour in employment relationship and within the employment environment. Failure to keep employment records, so that an objective assessment can be made as to whether an employee has received their minimum entitlements, was inconsistent with good faith behaviour and fundamentally undermined the trust and confidence inherent in the employment relationship. Other objects set out in s 3 of the Act are to acknowledge and address the inherent inequality of power in employment relationships, and also to promote the effect of enforcement of employment standards.10 Nature of the breaches Mr Dai’s failure to keep any employment records for Mr Chen or to provide him with a written employment agreement involved ongoing breaches of employment standards that continued for the duration of his employment. The failure to pay Mr Chen 7 Borsboom v Preet PVT Ltd [2016] NZEmpC 143. 8 Nicholson v Ford [2018] ERNZ 393. 9 A Labour Inspector v Daleson Investments Ltd [2019] NZEmpC 12. 10 Section 3(a)(ii) and 3(ab) of the Act. his annual holiday pay is also an ongoing breach that has continued since 25 August 2023. Maximum potential penalty The maximum penalty for each breach by an individual such as Mr Dai is $10,000.00. Sections 62 and 130 of the Act and s 27 and 81 of the HA03 have been breached, so there are four ongoing breaches in total, meaning the maximum potential total penalty that could be imposed was $40,000.00. Globalisation Because two of the breaches that attracted penalties involved Mr Dai’s failure to keep employment records, even though those obligations occurred under different legislation, it was appropriate to reduce these two breaches into one globalised breach for the purposes of assessing penalties. Globalisation therefore reduced the four breaches to three breaches, which can be summarised as failures to keep employment records, provide a written employment agreement and to pay annual holiday pay when Mr Chen’s employment ended. That reduced the potential maximum penalty from $40,000 to $30,000. Were the breaches deliberate, negligent or inadvertent? The breaches were likely negligent. At the time the breaches occurred Mr Dai was the sole director of Construst, so he was personally aware it had obtained Accredited Employer Work Visa status. As such Mr Dai should have been aware of minimum code legislation, because Construst had been granted 20 work visa tokens by Immigration New Zealand around the time Mr Chen was employed by Mr Dai. Mr Dai had also run other businesses which had employed employees. He therefore ought to have known what his legal obligations were to Mr Chen regarding his employment. Mr Dai’s failure to meet his legal obligations as an employer was negligent. Impact of the breaches Mr Dai’s breaches of employment standards had a seriously adverse impact on Mr Chen, because his attempts to assert his legal rights resulted in Mr Dai deciding not to give Mr Chen any more work. It therefore resulted in Mr Chen’s unexpected unjustified dismissal, which had seriously adverse impact on Mr Chen, his family and their financial situation. Mitigation Mr Dai has not taken any steps to mitigate the adverse effects his breaches have had on Mr Chen. Previous penalties Mr Dai has previously had a penalty imposed on him for aiding and abetting breaches of employment standards in relation to another employee (Mr Jiao) who was employed by Construst.11 However, the Authority noted that the conduct in issue in this matter pre-dated the imposition of a penalty on Mr Dai in Jiao v Construst and Dai.12 This was therefore not a situation in which a penalty had been imposed on Mr Dai, who then subsequently repeated the same breaches. Culpability There is a high level of culpability. Mr Dai has run multiple businesses. He should have known what his legal obligations were. Even if he did not know, he could and should have obtained advice about that when Mr Chen raised concerns with him (Mr Dai). Consistency It is important that the penalty imposed in this matter was consistent with other cases involving similar breaches of employment standards. The Authority was satisfied that has occurred. Mr Dai’s ability to pay Mr Dai did not provide any evidence regarding his (in)ability to pay a penalty, so this is a neutral factor. 11 Jiao v Construst and Dai [2024] NZERA 530. 12 Jiao, above n11. Need for deterrence Penalties must be set at a level that will act as a deterrence to Mr Dai personally. Penalties also need to be sufficient to deter other employers more generally, who could be inclined to be lax regarding their compliance with employment standards and minimum code legislation. The level of penalty therefore has to send a strong signal to all employers throughout New Zealand that their business practices must uphold minimum code obligations, some of the most important of which is providing a written employment agreement, keeping accurate employment documentation and paying an employee correctly. Amount of penalties imposed on Mr Dai After considering all of these factors, Mr Dai is ordered to pay a total penalty of $2,750.00. This consisted of: (a) A globalised penalty of $1,000.00 on Mr Dai for breaching s 130 of the Act and s 81 of the HA03; (b) A penalty of $1,000 for breaching s 65 of the Act, being his failure to provide a written employment agreement; and (c) $750 for failing to pay Mr Chen his annual holiday pay when his employment ended. Proportionality It is important that the total penalty imposed was not disproportionate to the nature and extent of the breaches that Mr Dai is being punished for. The Authority was satisfied that overall the penalty imposed was proportional to the extent of the wrongdoing that has occurred. Should some of the penalty be paid to Mr Chen? Pursuant to s 136(2) of the Act, the Authority may order all or part of any penalty imposed to be paid to any person instead of, or as well as, the Crown. Mr Chen has been put to the time and expense of bringing these breaches to the Authority’s attention. It was therefore appropriate for Mr Dai to pay $1,500.00 of the total $2,750.00 penalty imposed to Mr Chen directly, to recognise the harm Mr Chen has personally suffered as a result of the breaches that occurred, for which he cannot be compensated. Was Mr Chen dismissed? A dismissal happens when the ending of the employment relationship occurs at the employer’s initiative. Mr Chen did not resign. He was ready willing and available to attend work, but could not do so because no work was given to hm to do. Mr Chen’s employment ended when Mr Dai decided not to give him any more work to do. Without work to do Mr Chen was not paid. Mr Dai’s advice to Mr Chen to go elsewhere if he wanted full time employment also indicated there had been a dismissal. Mr Chen was a permanent full time employee. Mr Dai was therefore obliged to provide him with work to do or if he was unable to provide work then Mr Dai still needed to pay Mr Chen who was ready willing and available to perform the work he had been employed to do. The failure of Mr Dai to assign Mr Chen any work to do effectively dismissed him. There was sufficient work to do, as was evident from the high number of recently employed employees from overseas who were working for Construst under AEWV work visas on the same construction site and projects Mr Chen was employed to work on. Alternatively, Mr Dai’s stance that PAYE was not going to be paid on Mr Chen’s wages and that Mr Chen was not going to be given a written employment agreement were fundamental breaches that made it reasonably foreseeable Mr Chen would not continue working in such circumstances. Mr Chen was therefore also able to establish he had been constructively dismissed, even if the failure to provide him with work had not amounted to an actual dismissal. Was dismissal justified? Justification is to be assessed in accordance with the justification test in s 103A of the Act. This required the Authority to objectively assess whether Mr Dai’s actions, and how he had acted, were what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances at the time Mr Chen was dismissed.13 A fair and reasonable employer is expected to comply with its statutory and contractual obligations. Failure to do so could undermine its ability to justify its actions and/or dismissal of an employee. That was the case here. Mr Dai breached his statutory and good faith obligations to Mr Chen. Mr Dai reacted to Mr Chen’s attempts to obtain a written employment agreement by deciding not to give him any more work to do. That was a unilateral decision that Mr Dai made without consultation with Mr Chen. Mr Dai’s actions, and how he acted, was not what a fair and reasonable employer could have done in all the circumstances.14 He was therefore unable to justify Mr Chen’s dismissal. Accordingly, Mr Chen’s unjustified dismissal personal grievance claim succeeded. What remedies should be awarded? Mitigation of loss Mr Chen appropriately mitigated his loss by obtaining new employment on 14 September 2023. Lost remuneration Section 128(2) of the Act requires the Authority to order an employer to pay an employee the lesser of the sum equivalent to their lost remuneration or to three months’ ordinary time remuneration. Mr Chen was out of work for 19 days from 26 August to 13 September 2023. During the investigation meeting the parties calculated, and agreed, that if Mr Chen was held to be an employee, then his actual lost remuneration (based on the hours he had worked while employed by Mr Dai) was $5,236.53 gross. Accordingly, Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen actual lost remuneration of $5,236.53 gross under s 128(2) of the Act. 13 Section 103A(2) of the Act. 14 Above, n7. Distress compensation Mr Chen gave evidence about the stress, humiliation and distress his unjustified dismissal caused him. His family was put under “great financial pressure” which caused him to be “extremely anxious”, as he was reliant on his wages to be able to pay his mortgage. Mr Chen was very disappointed he lost his job. He told the Authority he suffered “significant psychological stress” as a result of his dismissal. Mr Chen described how his ability to eat and sleep was adversely affected and how it had caused him to lose confidence in himself and become depressed. Mr Chen said he felt deceived as he had lost his job for no reason. Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen $20,000.00 under s 123(1)(c)(i) of the Act to compensate him for the humiliation, loss of dignity and injury to feelings his unjustified dismissal caused him. Should remedies be reduced to reflect contribution? Section 124 of the Act required the Authority to assess the extent to which, if any, the remedies Mr Chen has been awarded should be reduced to reflect any contribution he had to the situation that gave rise to his dismissal grievance. Contribution requires blameworthy conduct which has been proven on the balance of probabilities. Blameworthy conduct in this case was not established, so Mr Chen’s remedies were not to be reduced. Orders Within 28 days of the date of this determination, Mr Dai is ordered to pay Mr Chen $27,647.26 gross: (a) $760.00 wage arrears, consisting of unpaid annual holiday pay; (b) $80.00 unpaid petrol allowance arrears; (c) Interest of $70.73 on the amount of $840.00 (being the wage and petrol allowance arrears) that ran from 27 August 2023 (the date employment ended) to 17 January 2025, being the date of this determination; (d) $5,236.53 lost remuneration; (e) $20,000 distress compensation, without deduction (meaning this amount is tax free); (f) $1,500.00 partial penalty. Interest will continue to accrue on the amount of $910.73(consisting of the total wage and petrol allowance arrears of $840.00 plus $70.73, being interest to date) until that full amount plus all accrued ongoing interest has been paid to Mr Chen. All interest is calculated using the Civil Debt Calculator on the Ministry of Justice website. Within 28 days of the date of this determination Mr Dai is ordered to: (a) Pay a penalty of $1,250.00 directly to the Crown bank account; (b) Inform IRD that Mr Chen was employed by Mr Dai personally as an employee from 28 July 2023 to 27 August 2023; (c) Correctly calculate the PAYE and any other legally required deductions (such as ACC levy) that should have been made from Mr Chen’s earnings and remit those amounts in full to IRD under Mr Dai’s name as the employer against Mr Chen’s IRD number, as an employee. Mr Dai as Mr Chen’s employer is legally responsible for any penalties and/or interest IRD imposes due to Mr Chen’s tax on the wages he was paid from 28 July 2023 to 25 August 2023 not having been correctly paid by his employer. What costs should be awarded? Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, Mr Chen may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. From the date of service of that memorandum Mr Dai and Construst will then have 14 days to lodge any reply memorandum. On request by either party, an extension of time for the parties to continue to negotiate costs between themselves may be granted. The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.15 Rachel Larmer Member of the Employment Relations Authority 15 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1

operative_excerpt: t commissions are owing. Did Mr Renner breach his duty of good faith owed to Roberton Motors? Mr Renner signed an employment agreement on 31 August 2020. There are three clauses contained in the IEA which are relevant to the claim Robertson Motors makes against Mr Renner. These are as follows: 30 Confidential information 30.9 During the course of employment or after termination of employment with the employer, the employee shall not directly or indirectly make a record of, or divulge, or communicate to any other person, any information regarding the employer’s business, or any matters associated with the employer. When requested, the employee hereby agrees to sign a Statutory Declaration stating that they are collecting commercially sensitive and valuable information only to perform the tasks required by the employer, that the commercially sensitive and valuable information will not be passed to others during and after the term of employment. The employee also irrevocably agrees to sign a Statutory Declaration stating they have returned all copies, in any and every form, of all commercially sensitive and valuable information on the termination of employment with the employer. 40. Non-solicitation 40.1 The employee shall not at any time during the period of employment or for a period of six months after termination of employment, for whatever reason, either on the employee’s own account or for any other person, firm, organisation or company, solicit, endeavour to entice away from or discourage from being employed by the employer, any other employee or actual client/customer or prospective client/customer of the employer. An employee who breaches this clause may be subject to disciplinary sanctions including possible termination of employment. 41. Restraint of trade 41.1 During the employee’s employment with the company the employee will be privy to sensitive and confidential information relating to the company’s business, and the employee may be in a position to develop and maintain relationships on behalf of the company with clients and other business associates. In order to protect the company’s interests the employee agrees that for a period of (3, 6, 9 or 12 months) after the termination of employment, the employee will not, either indirectly or directly: i. Own, establish, purchase, obtain an interest in, control, render services to, be employed by or otherwise be involved with or engaged by, whether for reward or otherwise, any business or enterprise which competes directly or indirectly with the business of the company, its subsidiaries, associates or affiliates, in the (state area or region restraint is to cover) region; ii. Solicit, canvass, entice or encourage any employee of the company to leave the company or interfere in any way with the relationship between the company and its employees; iii. Solicit, canvass, entice, deal with or encourage any client who is or was at any time during the last twelve (12) months of employment a client or customer of the company with a view to obtaining the business of that person/business; or iv. Interfere in any way with the relationship between the company and its clients, customers and employees. Robertson Motors say that Mr Renner breached one or more of the above provisions because, whilst he was still employed by them, he: (a) Solicited ShinMaywa away from the exclusive agreement it had with Robertson Motors; (b) Provided email contacts for ShinMaywa personnel to a client of the respondent; (c) Solicited or endeavoured to entice away clients/customers and/or potential clients/customers from Robertson Motors; (d) Did things to the detriment of Robertson Motors by promoting the relationships of its competitors, customers and clients with ShinMaywa rather than protecting and promoting the relationship of Robertson Motors with ShinMaywa. Robertson Motors also say that Mr Renner breached the non-solicitation provisions set out above because he has continued to solicit and entice away clients/customers and potential clients and customers. Mr Renner resigned in writing by letter, which although was dated 31 August 2023 was forwarded on 31 July 2023. The letter advised that his last day of employment would be 8 September 2023. Up until 8 September 2023, Mr Renner owed duties of good faith to Robertson Motors and was also bound by the provisions of his IEA both in relation to non-solicitation and restraint, and also his duty of fidelity and loyalty. Robertson Motors complains that during April 2023 and May 2023 Mr Renner used his work phone to communicate with a Mr Dudson of AB Equipment, a customer and potential competitor. Mr Dudson provided Mr Renner with his work email address. Robertson Motors says that this is evidence that Mr Renner was attempting to introduce AB Equipment to ShinMaywa. However, this evidence does not indicate that Mr Renner was acting against the interests of Robertson Motors. The employment agreement and duties of fidelity and loyalty do not prohibit Mr Renner from exploring other alternatives. What he cannot do is breach the specific provisions of his employment agreement or his implied duties of fidelity and loyalty and take any action to his advantage which may damage Robertson Motors. Robertson Motors takes issue with the fact that Mr Renner set up a company originally called New Life Beginnings Limited but latterly called Purpose Vehicle Solutions Limited. There is nothing in law which stops Mr Renner making arrangements for life post the end of his employment with Robertson Motors. The evidence was that Mr Renner’s company did not trade in any event and was originally set up so that an investment property could be transferred to it. The fact that this did not happen is by the by. On 13 April 2023, Mr Renner provided Mr Nishikawa and Mr Hiroki Takenaka of ShinMaywa with Mr Dudson’s email address. Whilst there is insufficient evidence suggesting a breach of the non-solicitation and/or restraint provisions of the employment agreement, it is difficult to see how providing ShinMaywa with Mr Dudson’s email address could be in the interests of Robertson Motors. The evidence shows that following this, a meeting took place between Mr Dudson and representatives of ShinMaywa. An email response states “Looking forward to new collaboration with AB Equipment”. Mr Renner did not discuss this issue with Robertson Motors and was certainly not acting in their interests. At this period of time, he was still an employee and was certainly not being active and constructive in maintaining a productive employment relationship. On 1 August 2023, Mr Renner emailed ShinMaywa advising of his resignation. This elicited a response back to Mr Renner “It may be necessary to think of a way how to continue and grow our sales activities”. The email to ShinMaywa was sent with no reference to Robertson Motors. A purpose of the notice period when an employee resigns, is to give an employer a chance to advise customers, suppliers and others of the resignation and take steps to protect their business. Advising Robertson Motors of his resignation on 31 July 2023, and then one day later sending an email to ShinMaywa unbeknownst to his employer may not on its own be a breach of non-solicitation or restraint provision, but nonetheless was certainly not helpful to Robertson Motors and could be seen as a breach of Mr Renner’s duty of good faith and fidelity and loyalty to his employer. At the very least he should have raised with Robertson Motors that was what he intended to as undoubtedly there would have been steps Robertson Motors would have wished to take. On 3 August 2023, Mr Renner emailed Robertson Motors largest customer, again forwarding email addresses for people at ShinMaywa. This was done without the knowledge of Robertson Motors. Again, this email was sent whilst Mr Renner was an employee owing duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty to Robertson Motors. It is difficult to see how he could have thought sending such an email was advancing the interests of Robertson Motors. ShinMaywa and Robertson Motors had a distribution rights agreement. The agreement gave Robertson Motors exclusive rights to sell listed ShinMaywa products in New Zealand. On 7 August 2023, a week after Mr Renner had forwarded his letter of resignation, ShinMaywa gave Robertson Motors notice that it was ending that agreement, meaning that Robertson Motors would no longer have the exclusive rights to sell ShinMaywa products in the New Zealand market. It is difficult to conclude other than if Mr Renner had not advised ShinMaywa of his resignation, that agreement would not have terminated at that time. By advising ShinMaywa one day after he had resigned but, during a notice period, Mr Renner deprived Robertson Motors from having a discussion with ShinMaywa regarding the effect of Mr Renner’s resignation. It is difficult to see that Mr Renner could possibly have thought his actions in communicating with ShinMaywa were advancing the interests of Robertson Motors. Indeed it is clear the opposite was true. Mr Renner’s actions constitute a breach of his duty of fidelity and loyalty which he owed to Robertson Motors. Mr Phil Arras, Chief Executive of NHR Group, gave evidence that he had known Mr Renner for some 20 years and that they were friends. An email from Mr Arras to ShinMaywa stated: Ian Renner gave me your email and asked me to contact you about how we may be able to help Ian set up the ShinMaywa business in New Zealand and navigate around his restraint of trade for three months. There may be a couple of ways to assist via the business I work at or through myself. Mr Renner accepts that he had a discussion with Mr Arras. Mr Renner also said that he did not believe there was any restriction on him setting up a business to compete with Robertson Motors. Whilst it is clear that that was a misguided view, equally, it seems that Mr Renner did not set up a business which competed. Nonetheless, having a friend contact ShinMaywa to instigate discussions for ongoing business, breaches Mr Renner’s duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty owed to Robertson Motors. In providing the information he did to third parties, Mr Renner breached the provisions of his employment agreement prohibiting him from removing or copying any confidential or commercially sensitive information. It certainly also breaches Mr Renner’s implied obligations of fidelity and loyalty to his employer. Restraint provision Mr Renner did not breach the restraint provisions contained in his employment agreement. He was not employed by any enterprise which competed directly or indirectly with Robertson Motors. There was no evidence he solicited, canvassed, enticed or encouraged any employee of the company to leave the company or interfered in any way with the relationships between the company and its employees. The evidence before the Authority made it clear that he did not solicit, canvass, entice, deal with or encourage any client of Robertson Motors to leave the business, with a view to obtaining the business of that person/business. Although there was some evidence that Mr Renner did want to continue a relationship with ShinMaywa, he said that that was in respect of ShinMaywa products that was not part of the prior exclusive agreement between ShinMaywa and Robertson Motors. Nonetheless, there is evidence that Mr Renner had some intention to breach the restraint provisions. He said he did not feel there was any obstacle to him owning and establishing a business in competition but as it transpires, although he took some steps in that regard, he did not breach the restraint provisions, although that may have been his intention. Summary of findings Robertson Motors did not unlawfully suspend Mr Renner. It did, however, breach its duty of good faith and acted in a misleading and deceptive manner in giving Mr Renner one reason for why it wished to take his laptop and phone when in fact it had another, namely a wish to forensically examine the devices seeking evidence of serious misconduct. Robertson Motors is required to pay commission on sales instigated by Mr Renner during his employment but which were completed after his employment ended. Mr Renner breached his duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty which he owed to Robertson Motors. He did this by dealing with ShinMaywa and others in a manner clearly designed to further his own interests and not that of Robertson Motors. This occurred during a time he was still an employee of Robertson Motors. Mr Renner did not breach the restraint provisions contained in his employment agreement. Orders In respect of the repossession of the laptop and phone, Robertson Motors breached the duty of good faith it owed to Mr Renner. It deliberately deceived him; however, Mr Renner also breached the duties of good faith, fidelity and loyalty he owed to Robertson Motors. No loss was suffered by either party. Under these circumstances I decline to order a penalty against either party. Mr Renner is entitled to commission on sales he instigated prior to the termination of his employment but which were completed after his employment ended. The parties will need to work out and agree on what commission is due to Mr Renner. If the parties cannot reach agreement on this, then leave is reserved to return to the Authority which will hear evidence on quantum and issue a determination accordingly. Costs Costs are reserved. The parties are encouraged to resolve any issue of costs between themselves. If the parties are unable to resolve costs, and an Authority determination on costs is needed, either party may lodge, and then should serve, a memorandum on costs within 28 days of the date of this determination. The parties can anticipate the Authority will determine costs, if asked to do so, on its usual “daily tariff” basis unless circumstances or factors, require an adjustment upwards or downwards.1 Geoff O’Sullivan Member of the Employment Relations Authority 1 For further information about the factors considered in assessing costs see: www.era.govt.nz/determinations/awarding-costs-remedies/#awarding-and-paying-costs-1
